text: 55-year-old male bodybuilder. The patient has been experiencing weakness in his right arm for a few weeks, which has progressively worsened to the point of dropping objects. He also reports a recent unexplained weight loss of 17 pounds and has a history of diabetes. The patient admits to chronic alcohol use, heavy smoking, and anabolic steroid use.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you have any difficulty swallowing, speaking, or breathing, and have you noticed any weakness or numbness in your legs or face? I also need to know if you have experienced any muscle twitching, cramps, or changes in your sense of touch.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Weakness in the right arm. I also have Decreased sensation in the right arm, Dull aching and burning pain in the right arm, Significant weight loss.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you have any pain in your neck or shoulder, and does the weakness involve both upper and lower motor neuron signs, such as muscle atrophy and fasciculations? I need to rule out cervical radiculopathy or a brachial plexus lesion. REQUEST TEST: MRI of the Cervical Spine and Brachial Plexus.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the normal MRI, significant weight loss, and history of steroid use, I need to rule out systemic causes like malignancy or metabolic disorders. Do you have any night sweats, fevers, or noticeable muscle wasting in other parts of your body? REQUEST TEST: CT of the Chest, Abdomen, and Pelvis.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: CT of the Chest shows a solid mass at the apex of the right lung, suggestive of a tumor. CT of the Abdomen and Pelvis results are not provided in the current data.

speaker: Doctor
text: The apical lung mass strongly suggests a Pancoast tumor causing brachial plexus compression. I need to assess for Horner's syndrome to confirm the diagnosis. Do you have any drooping of the right eyelid, a smaller right pupil, or decreased sweating on the right side of your face? REQUEST IMAGES

text: The denial of autonomic symptoms makes classic Pancoast syndrome less likely, but the apical mass is highly suspicious for a lung malignancy. speaker: Doctor
text: The normal brain MRI rules out metastasis, but the lung mass remains a critical finding that could be invading the brachial plexus directly.
